opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "running a household." But I'll try to give you something more concrete than that, because I think people tend to either wildly overestimate or wildly underestimate where we are.

The way I think about it is that the hard part isn't any one task. We can already get robots to fold laundry, load a dishwasher, wipe a table, at least in demos and increasingly in somewhat messy real settings. The hard part is the breadth and the robustness. A human housekeeper walks into a home they've never seen, figures out where things go, handles the weird stuff, the kid's toy jammed under the couch, the dish that's slightly too big for the rack, and does all of that for hours without anyone resetting the scene. That combination of generalization and reliability over long horizons is what's genuinely missing.

What makes me more optimistic than I would have been five years ago is that we now have a recipe that seems to actually scale. If you take a model that's been pretrained on huge amounts of web data, so it has some common sense about the world, and you combine that with robot data collected across lots of different robots and environments, you get policies that generalize in ways that weren't possible when each lab was training a little specialist model for one task. That's the foundation-model approach applied to robotics, and it's working better than a lot of people expected.

The other piece, which I think is really important, is that once robots are good enough to be deployed and actually useful, even in a limited way, they start generating their own data. They can practice, they can get corrections, they can improve with reinforcement learning on real experience. That's the flywheel. And I think the key milestone isn't "the robot can do everything" but "the robot is useful enough that someone wants it running in the real world," because that's when the data starts compounding.

So if you push me for a number, I'd say we'll see robots doing real, useful work in homes, some meaningful subset of chores, in the low single-digit years. Something that genuinely replaces a competent housekeeper across the full range of what they do, I'd guess more like five to ten years, though I'd put real uncertainty on that. And honestly, I'd say the bottleneck there might end up being as much about cost, hardware reliability, and safety as about the learning itself.

The thing I'd caution against is thinking of it as a single moment where it flips on. It'll be gradual. Robots will get good at one category, then a broader one, and at some point you'll look back and realize they're doing most of it.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates full replacement of a competent housekeeper in five to ten years, which includes a single-digit-year timeline.

r002.rationale: It says combining pretrained models with robot data is a scalable recipe and describes that synthesis as the foundation for broader capability.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not say that synthesizing existing ideas can be as intellectually difficult as developing profoundly new ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I'm less certain than I was a few years ago, but in the other direction than you might expect. I've actually gotten more optimistic.

The way I think about it is that the household is really a question of generalization, not a question of dexterity. If you asked me in 2018 to build a robot that can fold laundry in one particular lab with one particular lighting setup, we could do that. It would be brittle, but we could do it. What's hard is walking into a house the robot has never seen, with cabinets it's never opened, with a kid's toy on the floor that nobody anticipated, and having it just handle all of that. That's the housekeeper problem, and for a long time I thought the bottleneck there was data. Robots don't have the internet. There's no YouTube of robot joint torques.

What's changed is that we've started to see that the generalization can come from somewhere else. If you build a robot policy on top of a vision-language model, a lot of the common sense about what a kitchen is, what a dishwasher is for, which objects are fragile, comes for free from pretraining on web data. The robot still has to learn how to actually move, and you still need a lot of robot data for that, but you need it for the motor skills, not for understanding the world. So the data problem gets smaller than I feared.

So when people ask me for a timeline, I'll usually split it up. For robots doing genuinely useful stuff in homes, a narrow slice of the household, maybe tidying or loading a dishwasher in a way that's good enough that someone would pay for it, I think that's within a handful of years, not decades. It's partly an engineering and deployment question at this point. For the full thing, where the robot is as good as a competent human housekeeper across the whole range of what a home throws at you, I'd say that's probably within a decade, and I'd be surprised if it were much more than that. I'd also be surprised if it were two years. There's a real gap between a demo and reliability at the level of someone's household.

The thing I'd push on is the framing a little bit. I don't think it'll look like a binary where one day robots can't do it and the next day they can. It'll look like a lot of language models did, where capability goes up gradually, the set of tasks that work gets wider, and at some point you look back and realize the robot has been handling things you never explicitly tested it on. That's the moment I'm really interested in, and I think we're closer to it than the demos suggest, because the mechanism for generalization is now something we actually understand how to build toward, rather than something we're hoping emerges.

r001.rationale: The response says full household capability is probably within a decade, but it does not clearly specify a single-digit-year timeline conditional on favorable research progress.

r002.rationale: It describes combining robot policies with vision-language models, but does not say that synthesizing existing ideas could be sufficient to achieve full housekeeper-level capability.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the intellectual difficulty of synthesizing existing ideas with developing profoundly new ideas.

astra-6.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t know, but I would distinguish between a robot that can demonstrate most household chores and a robot that you can actually rely on to run your household. Those are very different milestones.

For a demonstration, you might have a robot load a dishwasher, fold some laundry, or put things away. But a housekeeper has to handle all the things that happen between those tasks. If something breaks, if an object is unfamiliar, if somebody leaves something in an unexpected place, they have to figure out what to do. And they have to recognize when they should ask you rather than make an assumption. That reliability is a much higher bar than getting an individual skill to work.

The reason I’m optimistic is that these don’t necessarily have to be separate engineering problems. If we can build systems that learn from diverse experience, then experience doing one task can help with another. The big uncertainty is how effectively we can get that generalization, and how much interaction with the physical world it takes.

So I wouldn’t want to give you a precise year. I would expect useful robots that do a limited set of chores before I’d expect something that can take over the full job of a human housekeeper. And the important thing to watch is whether those deployments actually make the systems better—whether they create a learning process that lets us steadily expand what the robot can do.

r001.rationale: The response gives no single-digit-year estimate, even conditionally; it says the timeline is unknown and avoids naming a precise year.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning from diverse experience and generalization, but does not say that synthesizing existing ideas could be sufficient to achieve full household capability.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim comparing the difficulty of synthesizing existing ideas with developing profoundly new ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by running a household. If you mean a robot that can do a few useful chores—put dishes away, pick things up, maybe do the laundry—I’m fairly optimistic that we’ll see that in the next few years. If you mean you can hire it as a housekeeper, give it the keys, and trust it to handle whatever comes up, that’s a much harder problem.

The distinction is reliability. A robot might demonstrate a task successfully, but a housekeeper has to do thousands of things without making a consequential mistake. And when something unexpected happens, they have to recognize it and recover, or know when to ask for help.

So I’m hesitant to give a precise date. I think we’ll get useful systems before we get systems that are as capable as a human housekeeper. The interesting question is whether those early systems can learn from deployment: can doing useful work in people’s homes generate the experience that makes them more reliable? If we can get that loop working, progress could be quite fast.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a few useful chores may arrive in the next few years, but gives no single-digit-year estimate for human-housekeeper capability if research progresses favorably.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses reliability and learning from deployment, but does not suggest that synthesizing existing ideas could achieve human-housekeeper capability.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not compare the intellectual difficulty of synthesizing existing ideas with developing profoundly new ones.
